practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a recognised user group in sport?
A) Middle-class adults
B) People with disabilities
C) Healthy people
D) Busy families
practice_questions.marks: B) People with disabilities [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two user groups who may have limited time available for sport and physical activity.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct answers from: people who work full-time / single parents / carers / families with children (accept any two that are genuinely different — answers that merely restate the same idea, e.g. 'people who are busy' and 'people who work', score only 1 mark). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why teenagers may be less likely to participate in sport than young children.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks. A simple point scores 1 mark (e.g. 'teenagers face peer pressure'). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. 'teenagers may feel self-conscious about their body or ability in front of friends, reducing their confidence to try new activities'). A further developed reason with an applied example or second distinct explanation scores 3 marks (e.g. add 'the transition from school sport to community clubs at age 16 means many teenagers fall out of organised activity entirely, as clubs can feel unwelcoming without a school-based entry point'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by the user group 'economically disadvantaged'. Give one example of how this affects their participation in sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): economically disadvantaged people have a low household income / cannot easily afford the costs associated with sport, such as club fees, kit or transport (2 marks for a clear, developed description; 1 mark for a basic statement).
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, a family may not be able to afford a gym membership or the cost of a child's football kit and registration fee, meaning the child cannot join a local club (2 marks for a specific, applied example; 1 mark for a vague example). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
Riverside Leisure Centre is redesigning its programme to attract more retired people and people over 60. At the moment, only 8% of its members are from this user group.

Discuss the factors a leisure centre manager should consider when trying to increase participation among retired people and people over 60.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two relevant factors from both sides or two perspectives, with specific examples applied to the scenario. For example: the need for low-impact, age-appropriate activities such as aqua aerobics or walking netball alongside the importance of social atmosphere; contrasted with the challenge that health conditions or lack of confidence may prevent this group from attending even well-designed sessions. Both factors are developed with reasoning.
Secure (3–4 marks): At least two relevant factors identified and briefly explained with some reference to the scenario context.
Developing (2 marks): One or two factors identified but not clearly explained or applied to the scenario.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Springvale Sports Club has noticed that carers in the local area rarely use their facilities. The club wants to develop a targeted programme to increase participation among this user group.

Evaluate the extent to which understanding the specific needs of carers can help a sports club increase participation rates among this user group.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation that identifies carers’ specific needs (very limited time, financial pressure, difficulty leaving the person they care for), argues that understanding these needs allows the club to design appropriate solutions (respite sessions, flexible timetabling, subsidised fees), and then challenges this with the counter-argument that even perfectly targeted provision may not overcome the most fundamental barrier (the carer may simply be unable to leave the dependent individual). A clear, substantiated judgement is reached that goes beyond listing points.
Secure (5–6 marks): At least two relevant points on each side (or two well-developed points and one on the other side), with some application to the scenario and an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points identified but largely one-sided or without a clear judgement. Some reference to carers but limited specificity.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points about carers or barriers with little development and no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a barrier to participation in sport?
A) High media coverage of women's sport
B) Lack of disposable income
C) Availability of concessionary pricing
D) Strong role models
practice_questions.marks: B) Lack of disposable income [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two solutions a sports club could use to increase participation among people with disabilities.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct answers from: pool hoists / wheelchair-accessible changing rooms / hearing loops / braille signage / adapted equipment / disability-specific coaching / adapted programmes such as sitting volleyball / wheelchair basketball. Accept any two genuinely different answers. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a lack of role models acts as a barrier to participation for ethnic minorities.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks. 1 mark for a basic point (e.g. 'if there are no role models from that background, people may feel the sport is not for them'). 2 marks for development (e.g. 'if ethnic minority young people do not see athletes from their background succeeding in a sport, they may not believe they could succeed themselves, which reduces motivation to try'). 3 marks for a fuller explanation or a second distinct reason applied to ethnic minorities (e.g. add 'in addition, clubs may seem culturally unfamiliar if all the coaches and committee members are from a different background, which reinforces the sense of not belonging'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the barrier of 'lack of transport' and explain one solution a sports club could offer to overcome this barrier for unemployed people.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): lack of transport means that people cannot get to sports facilities because they live far away, have no car, or public transport is limited or unavailable at the times sessions are held (2 marks for clear description; 1 mark for a basic statement).
Solution with example (up to 2 marks): the club could organise a minibus to collect members from a central meeting point, funded by a community grant, which removes the transport cost and logistics barrier for unemployed people who may not be able to afford a car or taxi (2 marks for a clear, applied solution; 1 mark for a vague suggestion). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
Ferndale Leisure Trust has identified that participation among single parents in their local area is very low. They have a limited budget.

Discuss the barriers single parents face when trying to participate in sport and how the leisure trust could overcome them.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A developed discussion that names at least two specific barriers (e.g. family commitments, lack of disposable income, lack of suitable provision) and matches each to a realistic solution within a limited budget (e.g. crèche provision on-site, concessionary pricing, taster sessions at no cost, family swim sessions). Both barriers and solutions are clearly linked and the answer considers more than one perspective or challenge.
Secure (3–4 marks): At least two barriers identified with some linked solutions, though development may be uneven.
Developing (2 marks): One barrier and one solution, or two barriers with no solutions.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Northgate Athletics Club has applied for a grant to improve participation among economically disadvantaged young people aged 11–16 in their town. The club is considering offering free taster sessions, subsidised kit loans, and a minibus from the town centre.

Evaluate how effective these three strategies are likely to be at removing the barriers faced by economically disadvantaged teenagers.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation that assesses all three strategies, explaining the specific barrier each targets (cost of trying, cost of kit, transport) and weighing effectiveness. The best answers argue that taster sessions remove the awareness and psychological barrier but not the ongoing cost barrier; subsidised kit loans address one major cost but not ongoing club fees; the minibus removes transport but only for those who know about the club and want to attend. A substantiated judgement is reached on which combination is most effective or what additional strategy would be needed.
Secure (5–6 marks): Two or more strategies evaluated with clear reasoning and some attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Strategies described but evaluation is one-sided or judgement is missing.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points about barriers or solutions with no evaluation. [8 marks]

before.exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to ‘suggest a solution to a barrier’, make sure your solution directly addresses the barrier you named — not just any barrier. For example, if the barrier is ‘lack of transport’, a relevant solution is ‘a club minibus scheme’; saying ‘build more facilities’ would not directly remove the transport barrier and will not score. For ‘discuss’ questions, consider two or more user groups or two or more barriers — examiners reward answers that consider more than one viewpoint.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes an 'emerging sport'?
A) A sport that has been established for over 50 years
B) A sport that is new or rapidly growing, seeking to establish clubs and competition structures
C) A sport that only elite athletes can participate in
D) A sport played outdoors only
practice_questions.marks: B) A sport that is new or rapidly growing, seeking to establish clubs and competition structures [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two factors that influence the popularity of a sport in the UK.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any two correct factors from: number of people participating / provision of facilities / environment and climate / live spectator opportunities / media coverage and range / high-level success / positive role models / social acceptability. (Both must be named to earn the mark; one alone scores 0.) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain how media coverage can affect the popularity of a sport.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks. 1 mark for a basic point (e.g. 'media coverage increases the number of people who know about a sport'). 2 marks for development (e.g. 'when a sport is broadcast on free-to-air television, millions of viewers become familiar with it, making them more likely to want to try it'). 3 marks for a further developed point with a specific example (e.g. add 'the BBC's Wimbledon coverage reaches around 9 million viewers and produces a documented spike in junior tennis sign-ups in the weeks after the tournament'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by 'social acceptability' in sport and give one example of how changing social acceptability has affected a sport's popularity.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): social acceptability refers to whether a sport is seen as normal, respectable and suitable for different groups in society, including particular genders, age groups or cultures (2 marks for a clear definition; 1 mark for a basic statement).
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, women's boxing was seen as socially unacceptable for much of the 20th century; changing attitudes and its inclusion at the Olympics from 2012 onward gradually made it acceptable and led to significant growth in female boxing participation (2 marks for a specific, applied example; 1 mark for a vague reference). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
Keston Racquets Club is considering adding a padel court to its facilities. The club secretary believes padel could grow membership significantly within three years.

Discuss the factors that could affect whether padel increases in popularity at Keston Racquets Club and in the wider UK.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two factors on each side. For example, factors supporting growth: easy to learn, social, growing media coverage, Sport England investment in facilities; factors that could limit growth: high cost of building a padel court, limited coaching availability, public unfamiliarity with the rules, competition from established racket sports. Both sides are clearly developed and applied to the scenario.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two or more relevant factors with some development, but balance may be uneven.
Developing (2 marks): One or two points with limited development.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Harrow Vale Leisure Trust is writing a report on why swimming is one of the most popular sports in the UK, while volleyball remains much less popular despite being an Olympic sport. The trust wants to use the report to make decisions about facility investment.

Evaluate the factors that explain why participation rates differ so much between swimming and volleyball in the UK.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A structured evaluation that addresses multiple popularity factors and applies them to both sports. Strong answers will note that swimming benefits from dedicated facility provision (public pools), year-round indoor participation, strong school curriculum presence, and visible elite success (Paralympic gold medals); while volleyball lacks dedicated facilities (shares sports halls with other sports), has limited free-to-air TV coverage, few nationally recognised British role models, and lower social acceptability as a recreational activity compared to swimming. The answer considers whether facility provision or media coverage is the most significant factor with a clear, substantiated judgement.
Secure (5–6 marks): At least two popularity factors applied to both sports with some judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Factors identified for one sport only, or applied without comparing the two sports.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points about popularity with no comparison or judgement. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a sporting value as defined in the specification?
A) Competitiveness
B) Aggression
C) Excellence
D) Determination
practice_questions.marks: C) Excellence [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two sporting values that relate to how athletes treat others on and off the field of play.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: fair play / tolerance and respect / citizenship / inclusion. (Accept any two genuine and distinct answers. 'Team spirit' focuses on internal group cohesion rather than treatment of others so should be marked with care — credit if the student explains it in terms of mutual support.) [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by the sporting value of 'citizenship' and give one example from sport.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks. 1 mark for a basic definition ('citizenship is about giving back to the wider community'). 2 marks for a developed definition ('citizenship means athletes and clubs using their platform and skills to contribute positively to society beyond sport'). 3 marks for adding a specific example ('for example, a Premier League club that runs free football sessions in a deprived area to reduce youth crime is demonstrating citizenship by using sport as a tool for social good'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the sporting value of 'national pride' and give one example of how it is expressed in a major sporting event.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): national pride is a sense of pride in one's country that is expressed through supporting national teams and athletes; sport provides a setting where people from different backgrounds find shared identity through representing or cheering for their nation (2 marks for a developed description; 1 mark for a basic statement).
Example (up to 2 marks): at the 2024 Paris Olympics, athletes across many sports competed under the British flag; hearing the national anthem at a medal ceremony and seeing athletes from diverse backgrounds celebrated as national heroes both expressed and created national pride among millions of viewers (2 marks for a specific, applied example; 1 mark for a vague reference). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
Westbourne Harriers is a community athletics club. A group of parents have complained that the club cares only about winning and that younger, less able athletes are being made to feel unwelcome. The club coach argues that pursuing excellence is the most important value in sport.

Discuss whether excellence should be the priority in a community sports club, or whether other values should take precedence.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A developed discussion that presents both sides clearly. Arguments for excellence as priority: high standards attract better athletes, produce results, and create role models; athletes who do not strive to improve may undermine the competitive culture of the club. Arguments for other values taking priority: inclusion and team spirit ensure all ability levels feel welcome; a community club has a social responsibility beyond results; fair play and citizenship matter to the club's reputation and its links with local schools. The answer considers more than one perspective and may reach a justified view.
Secure (3–4 marks): Both sides identified with some development, but balance may be uneven.
Developing (2 marks): One side only, or two points without development.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Bridgewater FC is a semi-professional women's football club in a medium-sized UK town. Over the past season, the club has experienced two serious incidents: one player received racial abuse from opposing supporters, and a match was abandoned after a brawl involving players from both teams.

Evaluate how far sport genuinely promotes the values of tolerance and respect and fair play, using the scenario above and your own sporting knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation that uses the Bridgewater FC scenario alongside broader knowledge. Arguments that sport promotes these values: governing bodies mandate fair play codes, referees enforce rules punishing disrespect (yellow cards, bans), campaigns like No Room For Racism actively tackle discrimination, and many athletes model exemplary behaviour on and off the pitch. Arguments that sport fails to promote these values: the two incidents at Bridgewater FC show that rules and campaigns have not eliminated abuse or violence; research suggests gamesmanship (time-wasting, simulation) is widespread at elite level; media coverage of poor conduct may normalise it. A substantiated judgement concludes how far sport promotes these values overall — for example, 'sport provides the framework for these values but cannot guarantee them; the behaviour of participants ultimately depends on individual character and club culture.' No judgement = cannot reach Mastering.
Secure (5–6 marks): Both sides developed with the scenario and broader examples; judgement present but may be thin.
Developing (3–4 marks): Points made but one-sided or judgement missing.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a Paralympic value?
A) Friendship
B) Respect
C) Excellence
D) Courage
practice_questions.marks: D) Courage [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify the three Olympic values.
practice_questions.marks: All three must be named to score the mark: Excellence, Respect, Friendship. [1 mark for all three correct; 0 if any are missing or replaced with a Paralympic value]

practice_questions.text: Explain what the five interlocking rings of the Olympic symbol represent.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks. 1 mark for 'the five rings represent five continents'. 2 marks for development: 'the five interlocking rings represent the five continents of the world — Africa, the Americas, Asia, Europe and Oceania — whose athletes come together at the Games; the interlocking design represents unity'. 3 marks for adding the colour point: 'the five colours (blue, yellow, black, green and red) plus white were chosen because every national flag in the world contains at least one of these six colours, symbolising universal participation'. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the Paralympic value of 'Inspiration' and explain one way it can be seen in sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): Inspiration is the power of Paralympic athletes to change attitudes toward disability in society, encouraging people with disabilities to take part in sport and challenging non-disabled people to reconsider what the human body can achieve (2 marks for a developed description; 1 mark for a basic statement).
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, the gold medal performance of a British blind triathlete at Paris 2024 was cited by disability charities as triggering a significant increase in enquiries to para-triathlon clubs, showing how elite success directly inspires grassroots participation (2 marks for a specific applied example; 1 mark for a vague reference). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
Oakfield Academy runs a sports day for Year 9 students. The head of PE wants to redesign the event so that it promotes Olympic and Paralympic values, not just competitive winning. The event currently awards medals only for finishing first, second and third.

Discuss how Oakfield Academy could redesign its sports day to promote Olympic and Paralympic values across the whole event.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A developed discussion covering at least two values from each movement with specific redesign proposals. For example: add a sportsmanship award to embed Respect; introduce team relay events where all ability levels are mixed to promote Friendship; include events specifically for students with disabilities to promote Equality and Courage; reward consistent effort over the year to embody Excellence and Determination. The answer considers both what to add and potential challenges (cost, time, student buy-in), and presents more than one viewpoint.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two or more values named with some linked suggestions, but coverage may be thin.
Developing (2 marks): One value mentioned with one suggestion, or two values without proposals.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Clayfield Sports College has been invited to host an Olympic Values Day for local primary schools. The college must design activities that bring the Olympic Creed and at least two Olympic values to life for pupils aged 9 and 10.

Evaluate how effectively an Olympic Values Day could promote the Olympic Creed and the values of Excellence and Friendship among primary school pupils, considering both what could be achieved and the challenges involved.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation that identifies how the Creed and both values could be promoted (e.g. design activities where participation and effort are rewarded over results, linking directly to 'not to win but to take part'; mixed-school team challenges that require co-operation across strangers to build Friendship; achievement ladders rather than league tables for Excellence). The answer then challenges these by arguing that competitive children and teachers accustomed to results-based sport may resist non-competitive framing; that a single day is insufficient to embed values; that without follow-up in PE lessons the impact fades. A clear, substantiated judgement concludes how effective such a day could be — acknowledging that it creates awareness but that sustainable promotion requires curriculum embedding. No judgement = cannot reach Mastering.
Secure (5–6 marks): Two or more arguments on each side with some development; judgement present.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points but one-sided or no judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic description of the Creed or values with no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of sportsmanship?
A) A basketball player deliberately elbowing an opponent when the referee is not looking
B) A footballer kicking the ball out of play so an injured opponent can receive treatment
C) A tennis player bouncing the ball unusually slowly to unsettle a nervous opponent before serving
D) A rugby player disputing every decision made by the referee throughout the match
practice_questions.marks: B) A footballer kicking the ball out of play so an injured opponent can receive treatment [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two examples of negative spectator behaviour at a live sporting event.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for each genuinely distinct example (maximum 2 marks). Acceptable answers include:
- Throwing objects onto the pitch / at players or officials
- Pitch invasion / entering the field of play without permission
- Racist or abusive chanting directed at players
- Fighting between rival supporters
- Using pyrotechnics (flares, smoke bombs) in the crowd
- Verbally intimidating officials or players
Do not award a second mark if both answers are essentially the same point (e.g. 'shouting abuse' and 'chanting abuse').

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between sportsmanship and gamesmanship. Give one example of each.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for a clear definition of sportsmanship (playing within the letter and spirit of the rules / showing respect for the sport and opponents). Award 1 mark for a clear definition or description of gamesmanship (bending the rules / exploiting loopholes without technically breaking them). Award 1 mark for a relevant, applied example of each:
- Sportsmanship example: e.g. kicking the ball out for an injured player; shaking hands after a defeat; accepting a referee's call without complaint
- Gamesmanship example: e.g. time-wasting at a throw-in; bouncing the ball slowly before a serve; calling an injury to disrupt opposition momentum
All 3 marks can be awarded without mentioning both examples if the definitions are sufficiently precise and applied.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which poor spectator behaviour can negatively affect a sporting event. Give one example from sport to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Credit two distinct negative effects (up to 2 marks each) with development:
- Safety risks: fans may be injured or killed (e.g. crowd crushes, fighting). Reference to Hillsborough 1989 or similar crowd disaster is creditworthy.
- Match disruption / abandonment: incidents of pitch invasion, flares or serious fighting may force officials to stop play.
- Reputational damage: the sport or club is associated with disorder, deterring families, sponsors and broadcasters.
- Financial penalty: governing bodies can fine clubs, close grounds or impose points deductions following crowd trouble.
A named sporting example is required for the top marks on the second point. A generic answer with no named example is capped at 2 marks.

practice_questions.text:
Kingsmere FC is a non-league football club in Worcestershire. After a closely contested local derby, a group of away supporters entered the pitch and confronted home players. The club received a warning from the county FA.

Discuss how spectator behaviour, both positive and negative, can affect a football club like Kingsmere FC.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Balanced discussion covering both positive and negative spectator behaviour, with development of at least two distinct effects in each direction. Points are linked and interact (e.g. one negative consequence leads to another). Named or applied examples used. Judgement or synthesis attempted.

Secure (3-4 marks): At least two effects discussed, one positive and one negative, with some development beyond a simple list. Limited interaction between points.

Developing (2 marks): Two or more valid effects stated but with little development. May be one-sided (only positives or only negatives).

Emerging (1 mark): A single valid point about spectator behaviour with no development.

Credit points such as: positive atmosphere lifts player performance; community identity and belonging; negative behaviour leads to fines, ground closures, point deductions; physical safety risks; reputational damage to club and sport; impact on sponsorship and media coverage.

practice_questions.text: Give two examples of etiquette that might be observed in any sport of your choice.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per distinct and relevant etiquette example (maximum 2 marks). Answers must name or clearly describe a specific expected behaviour rather than a vague statement. Acceptable examples:
- Shaking hands with opponents / officials after a match
- Applauding good play by the opposing team or player
- Acknowledging when a ball was out that was called in (e.g. tennis)
- Kicking the ball out for an injured opponent in football
- Walking off the field promptly when given out in cricket
- Waiting for a break in play before collecting a stray ball (tennis / badminton)
Do not award if both examples are essentially the same behaviour described differently.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the role of WADA?
A) A UK-only body that tests athletes for banned substances at major competitions
B) An international organisation that sets the global Prohibited List and co-ordinates anti-doping testing across sport
C) A government department that decides on prison sentences for athletes caught doping
D) A sports court that hears appeals from athletes who fail drug tests
practice_questions.marks: B) An international organisation that sets the global Prohibited List and co-ordinates anti-doping testing across sport [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two reasons why an elite athlete might choose to use a performance-enhancing drug.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per distinct reason (maximum 2 marks). Acceptable answers include:
- Financial rewards / prize money available at elite level
- Competitive pressure (from coaches, sponsors, nation)
- Belief that rivals are already using PEDs
- Pressure to recover quickly from injury
- State-sponsored / institutional doping culture
- Desire to extend career as the body ages
Do not award a second mark for answers that are essentially the same point rephrased.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the Whereabouts Rule helps to deter doping in elite sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
- 1 mark: state what the Whereabouts Rule is (athletes must declare their location for one hour each day for unannounced testing)
- 1 mark: explain why this deters doping (testers can arrive without warning; athletes cannot time their drug use to avoid tests)
- 1 mark: apply or develop the point (e.g. three missed tests in 12 months equals a violation; out-of-competition testing catches substances used during training that clear the body by race day; athletes submit information quarterly via ADAMS)

practice_questions.text: Describe the sanctions an athlete might face if they tested positive for a banned substance. Use an example from sport to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Credit must cover the sanctions ladder AND include at least one named example:
- Warning / formal caution (minor or first-time breach)
- Fine
- Competition ban (length varies: 1 year to lifetime; 4-year ban standard for first serious offence under 2021 Code)
- Results annulment (medals, records, prize money returned)
- Criminal prosecution for trafficking
Named example (required for top marks): Sun Yang (extended ban for refusing cooperation with testers); Russian athletes competing as AIN at Paris 2024 following state-sponsored doping programme; any other accurately described real case. An answer with no named sporting example is capped at 2 marks.

practice_questions.text:
Riverside Harriers is an athletics club in Yorkshire. Their star 800m runner, Connor, is in the national Registered Testing Pool. Last year, testers visited three times when he was not at his declared location. He says he simply forgot to update his details.

Discuss whether education strategies alone are enough to prevent doping in sport, using the scenario above to help frame your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Balanced discussion that addresses at least two arguments in favour of education being sufficient AND at least one argument that testing/sanctions are also needed. Points interact: e.g. education raises awareness but determined cheaters require enforcement. The scenario is referenced or applied meaningfully. Development beyond a list.

Secure (3-4 marks): At least two valid points on different sides, with some development. Scenario may be referenced but not fully applied.

Developing (2 marks): Two or more valid points stated with limited development, likely one-sided.

Emerging (1 mark): A single valid point about education or anti-doping with no development.

Credit: education raises awareness early; role models are powerful; supplements education reduces inadvertent positives. BUT: financial incentives remain; determined cheaters will not be deterred by values alone; Whereabouts / testing catches those education misses; sanctions provide a real deterrent. The scenario shows that even administrative failings (not knowing/following the Whereabouts Rule) require enforcement not just education.

practice_questions.text:
'Performance-enhancing drugs should be legalised in elite sport so that athletes can compete on an equal footing.'

Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Sophisticated, balanced evaluation. Arguments for legalisation are presented fairly and fully (e.g. would create a level playing field if all could access the same substances; reduces hypocrisy of selective testing; athletes as consenting adults; difficult/expensive to police). Arguments against are equally developed (health risks, especially long-term; sets a damaging example for young and junior athletes; undermines the value of natural talent and training; access inequalities — wealthier athletes/nations could afford better drugs; erosion of sport's values). A clear, justified conclusion is reached, not just stated. Applied sporting example used (e.g. Russian state-doping scandal; Prohibited List enforcement).

Secure (5-6 marks): Clear argument on both sides with relevant evidence. A conclusion is present but may not be fully substantiated. Some applied context.

Developing (3-4 marks): Some argument on both sides. Evidence is limited or assertion-based. Conclusion may be missing or undeveloped.

Emerging (1-2 marks): One-sided answer or simple statements without evaluation. No real engagement with the counter-argument.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a 'regular and recurring' major sporting event?
A) The FIFA World Cup
B) The UEFA Champions League Final
C) The Summer Olympic Games
D) Wimbledon
practice_questions.marks:
D) Wimbledon [1 mark]
(Wimbledon is held every year at the same venue — the All England Club. The World Cup and Champions League Final are 'regular' events held in different locations. The Olympics is a 'one-off' event.)

practice_questions.text: State two positive impacts for a host city in the period before a major sporting event takes place.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per distinct positive (maximum 2 marks). Acceptable answers:
- Infrastructure development (new roads, rail, airports)
- Increased construction employment / job creation
- Commercial investment / business growth
- International profile / media attention raised pre-event
- Tourism bookings increase in advance of the event
- Urban regeneration of the host area
Do not award a second mark for the same point restated (e.g. 'jobs' and 'more workers employed' = 1 mark only).

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a 'one-off' and a 'regular' major sporting event. Give one example of each.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for correct definition of one-off (held in a host city once in a generation / same city very unlikely to host again for many decades). Award 1 mark for correct definition of regular (held repeatedly in different cities each time). Award 1 mark for a correct named example of each:
- One-off: Olympic / Paralympic Games, FIFA World Cup, Commonwealth Games
- Regular: UEFA Champions League Final, World Athletics Championships, Rugby World Cup
Do not award for 'Wimbledon' as a regular example — it is regular and recurring.

practice_questions.text: Describe two reasons why a city government might have concerns about bidding for the right to host the Summer Olympics. Use examples to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Credit two distinct concerns with development:
- Costs: hosting can require major public and private spending. Paris 2024’s Organising Committee had a final budget of about €4.48 billion, while the French Court of Auditors estimated public spending connected to the Games at €6.6 billion.
- Displacement and community disruption: building venues requires relocating residents, often from lower-income areas, who may receive inadequate compensation.
- Political opposition: public may resist via protest or referendum, causing reputational and governance problems for the host government.
- Bid cost with no guarantee: a bid campaign alone costs tens of millions; a losing city gets nothing back.
A named example is required for the top marks. An answer without any named example is capped at 2 marks.

practice_questions.text:
Thornfield City Council is considering bidding for the right to host a major international athletics championship. Some councillors are in favour; others are opposed.

Discuss the pre-event advantages and disadvantages a host city like Thornfield would need to consider before submitting its bid.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Balanced discussion addressing at least two distinct pre-event advantages and two distinct disadvantages. Points are developed and interact with each other (e.g. infrastructure benefit has to be weighed against cost of building it). Applied context used. Points are not just listed but linked into a reasoned argument.

Secure (3-4 marks): At least two valid points on each side with some development. Limited interaction between points. May not address all key areas.

Developing (2 marks): Two or more valid points identified but little development. One-sided or near-one-sided.

Emerging (1 mark): A single valid pre-event factor identified, with no development.

Credit: advantages — infrastructure (roads/rail/broadband), construction jobs, commercial investment, tourism bookings, raised national/city profile. Disadvantages — bid cost risk, construction cost overruns, displacement of residents, noise/disruption during build phase, political opposition from local community.

practice_questions.text: Identify two organisations that assess bids for major sporting events. For each organisation, name the event they award.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct organisation-event pairing (maximum 2 marks):
- IOC (International Olympic Committee) — awards the Summer and Winter Olympic Games
- FIFA — awards the FIFA World Cup
Also accept: IOC for Paralympic Games (awarded alongside the Olympics to the same host city).
Do not award for naming the organisation alone without its associated event.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a 'white elephant' in the context of major sporting events?
A) A venue that is sold to a private owner after the event for use as a concert hall
B) A stadium built for the Olympics that becomes a permanent home ground for a local football club
C) A purpose-built velodrome that is left empty and deteriorating after the Games
D) A temporary beach volleyball court dismantled after the event as planned
practice_questions.marks: C) A purpose-built velodrome that is left empty and deteriorating after the Games [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two positive impacts that occur during a major sporting event for the host city.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per distinct positive (maximum 2 marks). Acceptable answers:
- Increased tourism and visitor spending
- Short-term job creation (catering, security, stewarding, media)
- Boost to national morale / social cohesion
- Raised international profile / global media coverage
- Increased interest in and coverage of sport
Do not award a second mark for the same point described differently.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by 'legacy' in the context of hosting a major sporting event.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
- 1 mark: correct definition — the lasting, long-term effects that remain after a major sporting event has ended
- 1 mark: identification of an area of legacy (e.g. sporting facilities, transport infrastructure, participation rates, international reputation, financial impact)
- 1 mark: applied example (e.g. Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park remaining in use after London 2012; Athens 2004 venues falling into disrepair; Paris 2024 Seine-cleaning project benefiting Parisians)
A definition alone with no development earns 1 mark maximum.

practice_questions.text: Describe two negative legacies that can result from hosting the Olympic Games. Use examples from specific host cities to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Credit two distinct negative legacies with development:
- White elephant venues: purpose-built facilities that fall into disuse, as seen most starkly in Athens 2004 where most venues were abandoned within a decade.
- Financial burden: costs far exceeded revenue. Athens 2004 estimated at around £7-9bn, contributing to Greece's later fiscal crisis.
- Displacement without return: communities moved to make way for venues who do not benefit from post-event regeneration.
- Debt and austerity: host nation government may face years of debt repayment, diverting public funds from health, education or welfare.
Named example required for top marks. An answer with no named host city is capped at 2 marks.

practice_questions.text:
Riverton City is a medium-sized UK city that hosted a major athletics world championship three years ago. The new 50,000-seat athletics stadium is now used only for occasional concerts, and local athletics participation has not increased.

Evaluate whether the legacy of hosting a major sporting event is likely to be positive or negative for a host city like Riverton.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Sophisticated, balanced evaluation that addresses multiple dimensions of legacy (facilities, participation, economic, infrastructure, international profile). Arguments are developed beyond assertion. A named or applied example (London 2012, Athens 2004, or the Riverton scenario itself) is used to anchor points. A clear, justified conclusion is reached that links back to the question — e.g. 'legacy is likely to be positive only when reuse planning is embedded in the original bid, as London 2012 demonstrated; without this, white elephant and debt risks dominate as in Athens 2004.' Riverton scenario is engaged with meaningfully.

Secure (5-6 marks): Clear argument on both sides, at least two developed points in each direction. A conclusion is present but may not be fully substantiated. Named example likely present.

Developing (3-4 marks): Some argument on both sides, but development is limited and may be list-like. Conclusion present but underdeveloped. Named example may be absent.

Emerging (1-2 marks): One-sided or very thin answer. Little engagement with the question's specific context. No real evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Identify one positive impact on national morale during a major sporting event, and explain why this impact may not last once the event is over.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
- 1 mark: identify a positive morale impact (e.g. shared national pride in host nation's athletes winning medals; collective watching experience; sense of unity and celebration)
- 1 mark: explain why it may not last (morale is temporary / tied to event itself; once coverage ends, everyday social divisions and issues return; participation gains may not follow morale boosts if funding is not sustained)
- 1 mark: apply or develop (e.g. Team GB cycling medals at London 2012 boosted cycling interest but grassroots funding was later cut, limiting long-term participation growth)

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the National Governing Body for cricket in England and Wales?
A) The FA
B) The LTA
C) The ECB
D) The RFU
practice_questions.marks: C) The ECB (England and Wales Cricket Board) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two functions of a National Governing Body.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per distinct function (maximum 2 marks). Acceptable answers:
- Promoting participation in the sport
- Developing coaching standards and qualifications
- Developing officiating standards
- Organising competitions (national leagues, cups, etc.)
- Amending and enforcing the rules of the sport
- Supporting anti-doping / working with UKAD
- Providing insurance, technical guidance or safety standards
- Lobbying for funding from Sport England or UK Sport
Do not award a second mark for the same function rephrased.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which VAR (Video Assistant Referee) has improved football, and one way in which it has been criticised.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
- 1 mark: one benefit of VAR correctly described (e.g. eliminates clear and obvious errors in goals, penalties, red cards or mistaken identity; prevents incorrect results)
- 1 mark: one criticism correctly described (e.g. disrupts the flow of the game; long delays kill atmosphere; inconsistent interpretation of 'clear and obvious'; undermines officials' authority)
- 1 mark: development or application of either point (e.g. explaining why delayed celebrations reduce spectator enjoyment; naming the four categories VAR can review; explaining how frequent overturns erode referee confidence)

practice_questions.text: Describe how technology has helped to make sport safer for participants. Use a named example to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Credit must include at least two distinct safety-related uses of technology AND a named example:
- GPS/wearable vests monitor training load, heart rate and sprint speeds, reducing overtraining and injury risk in football and rugby
- Instrumented mouthguards in rugby measure head impacts and can alert medical staff to a possible concussion
- Prosthetic carbon-fibre limbs allow Paralympic athletes to compete with reduced injury risk and improved mobility (named: Paralympic sprint blades)
- Video analysis / slow-motion review allows medical teams to study injury mechanisms and inform prevention programmes
- Rule changes informed by data analysis (e.g. high-tackle restrictions in rugby, informed by concussion data from RFU medical teams)
A named example is required. An answer with no named technology is capped at 2 marks.

practice_questions.text:
Ferndale Rovers is a semi-professional football club in West Wales. Their chairman is considering investing in GPS performance vests for the squad and a basic video analysis system.

Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of introducing technology into a semi-professional football club like Ferndale Rovers.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Balanced discussion covering advantages and disadvantages, developed beyond assertion. Points interact (e.g. the data advantage must be weighed against the cost burden for a semi-professional club). The Ferndale scenario is applied meaningfully — advantages discussed in the context of a club at that level, not just elite sport. More than two distinct points on each side.

Secure (3-4 marks): At least two valid points on different sides with some development. Scenario referenced but not fully applied.

Developing (2 marks): Two or more valid points identified, likely one-sided or very thin development.

Emerging (1 mark): A single valid point about technology in sport with no development.

Credit advantages: injury risk reduction; improved coaching decisions; better understanding of player fitness; competitive edge. Credit disadvantages: high upfront cost for a semi-professional budget; ongoing subscription/maintenance costs; requires staff training to interpret data; risk of over-reliance on data over coach judgment; data privacy concerns for players.

practice_questions.text:
'Technology has done more harm than good for sport.'

Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Sophisticated evaluation presenting strong arguments on both sides. Arguments for (harm): VAR disrupts flow and atmosphere; cost creates inequality between elite and grassroots; frequent overturns undermine officials; data privacy risks. Arguments against (benefit): accurate decisions (Hawk-Eye, GoalLine tech); safety improvements (GPS load monitoring, concussion sensors); performance analysis unlocking athlete potential; enhanced spectator experience at broadcasts. A clear, justified conclusion is reached, not just stated — e.g. 'technology has improved accuracy and safety but has introduced unintended consequences for the spectator experience, particularly with VAR; on balance, the benefits outweigh the harms if technology is implemented thoughtfully.' Applied sporting examples used throughout.

Secure (5-6 marks): Clear argument on both sides with relevant examples. Conclusion present but may not be fully justified.

Developing (3-4 marks): Some argument on both sides; evidence limited or one-sided.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Single-sided answer or simple assertions with no real evaluation.
